title: Bug from stack trace workflow
summary: Use a stack trace to identify a testable failure location, reproduce the problem, evaluate a focused correction, and retain evidence that the correction worked.
prerequisites: The complete stack trace or the most complete copy available
Access to the source code associated with the reported failure
A way to repeat the operation that produced the failure

sections.title: Answer and source update
paragraphs: Where should you start when a stack trace is all you have? Preserve the complete trace, find the reported failure location, identify the nearest relevant frame in code you control, and use that location to form a hypothesis that you can reproduce before changing the code. Treat the trace as evidence about where the failure appeared, not as proof of its underlying cause.

This is an intermediate-level workflow for practitioners who can read source code and repeat a failing operation. The previous citation, content/resources/practical-workflow-recipes/bug-from-stack-trace-workflow.json, was an unregistered local publisher path and had never been verified. It has been replaced with the canonical arXiv record for The Debugging Book. This correction affects citation provenance and verification metadata only; the operational workflow remains unchanged.

sections.title: Investigation procedure
paragraphs: Step 1: Save the exact error message, the complete stack trace, the operation being attempted, and the input or state associated with the failure. If the trace is truncated, repeat the failing operation and capture a complete copy. If a complete copy cannot be obtained, record which portion is missing and continue only with conclusions that do not depend on that portion.

Step 2: Locate the failure position reported by the trace, then distinguish frames belonging to code you control from frames outside that code. Confirm that the available source corresponds to the code that produced the trace. If a reported location does not exist or does not match the available source, obtain the matching source or reproduction artifact before drawing a location-based conclusion. If that material is unavailable, record the location as UNKNOWN and request it.

Step 3: Form one testable hypothesis from the error message, the failing operation, the relevant frame, and the values entering that operation. Attempt the smallest reproduction that still produces the same failure. If the failure does not reproduce, capture another occurrence with the same contextual evidence rather than changing code speculatively. If several hypotheses remain possible, test one at a time so that each result has a clear interpretation.

Step 4: Apply the smallest correction that addresses the reproduced cause, then repeat the same reproduction and a related successful case. If the original failure remains, restore the prior behavior and revise the hypothesis using the new evidence. If the original case passes but the related case fails, revise or narrow the correction before accepting it.

sections.title: Expected evidence and verification
paragraphs: The expected evidence is a preserved trace, a confirmed mapping from the relevant frame to matching source, a reproducible failing case, a stated hypothesis, and before-and-after results from the same case. Verify the outcome by showing that the original reproduction fails before the correction and succeeds afterward under the same relevant conditions.

Also retain the result of at least one related successful case to check that the correction did not merely move the failure. If the original failure cannot be reproduced, the correction is not verified by this workflow. Mark the result unresolved and collect a new trace, matching source, inputs, and execution context from another occurrence before proceeding.
